cards.title: UN Climate Law Moves From Symbolic Norms Toward Enforceable State Pressure
cards.background: In 2024, the International Court of Justice issued an advisory opinion stating that states have a legal obligation to prevent significant harm to the climate system and that failure to do so carries legal consequences. Vanuatu, backed by a coalition spanning every region, had previously secured a UN General Assembly request for the opinion, which passed by consensus after 132 countries co-sponsored it. The current UN resolution seeks to give the advisory opinion practical effect by urging member states to uphold the ICJ’s obligations and by paving the way for follow-up action within the UN system.

prop_args.thesis: Endorsing the ICJ climate opinion through a UN resolution strengthens global climate governance by turning a moral claim into a durable legal and diplomatic obligation.
mechanisms: First, it converts a soft-law statement into a coordination focal point. This is because (1) states now have a common legal reference point for negotiations, (2) domestic courts and regulators can cite the opinion to justify stricter climate policy, and (3) repeated UN endorsement raises the reputational cost of non-compliance.

Second, it increases compliance pressure on high-emitting states without needing a new treaty. Three reasons: one, advisory opinions are often used to shape state behavior even when not formally binding; two, UNGA backing signals broad legitimacy across the international system; three, it gives climate-vulnerable states a stronger basis to shame, litigate, and mobilize against laggards.

Third, it protects the multilateral order at a moment of fragmentation. This matters because (1) if courts and UN bodies cannot translate legal findings into action, international law becomes performative, (2) small states like Vanuatu gain a rare institutional tool against power asymmetry, and (3) reinforcing rules-based cooperation is itself valuable in a world of bilateralism and great-power withdrawal.

opp_args.thesis: The resolution is mostly symbolic and risks overstating the enforceability of climate law while provoking backlash from major emitters.
mechanisms: First, it cannot create real enforcement where none exists. One, the ICJ opinion is advisory rather than binding, so states can ignore it at low immediate cost; two, the UN General Assembly cannot compel emissions cuts or impose sanctions; three, states already opposed to climate constraints will treat the resolution as political theater.

Second, it may harden resistance among powerful fossil-fuel states. One, public legal pressure can trigger sovereignty backlash and reduce cooperation in other forums like COP; two, governments facing domestic energy or industrial pressure may frame the resolution as external interference; three, adversarial framing can make future compromise harder by turning climate policy into a legitimacy contest.

Third, it can distract from more effective climate tools. One, emissions reductions depend more on finance, technology transfer, and domestic regulation than on declaratory UN texts; two, diplomatic energy spent on resolutions may crowd out practical bargaining over adaptation and funding; three, vulnerable states may gain headlines but not the material resources they actually need.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether symbolic legal pressure meaningfully changes state behavior or merely records existing norms. Prop is stronger if you believe legitimacy, litigation, and reputational costs matter in a fragmented system; Opp wins if you think major emitters can absorb the political cost and that only material incentives move emissions.
motion_areas: TH, as the UN General Assembly, would endorse the ICJ’s climate advisory opinion
THBT international courts should be used to enforce climate obligations
THP a world where climate-vulnerable states can use international law to pressure major emitters
THBT the UN should prioritize legal accountability over voluntary climate pledges

cards.title: US Tariff Rollback Triggers $35.5 Billion Refund Shock and Reopens the Trade War
cards.background: On May 12, 2026, Bloomberg reported that U.S. tariff refunds totaling $35.5 billion had been cleared for importers so far after the Supreme Court struck down the bulk of tariffs imposed by President Donald Trump the previous year. In response, Trump said he would sign an order imposing a 10% global tariff and pledged new investigations that could authorize additional import taxes. The article is set against a major legal and policy reversal in U.S. trade policy, with importers seeking repayment while the administration looks for new tariff tools.

prop_args.thesis: The tariff refund ruling weakens executive trade coercion and restores predictability for firms, lowering costs and reducing the hidden tax burden on consumers.
mechanisms: First, the refunds directly unwind a large distortion in input pricing. This is because (1) importers had already paid tariffs embedded into the cost of goods, (2) those costs were passed through into supply chains and retail prices, and (3) returning $35.5 billion gives firms immediate liquidity to reprice, restock, and invest rather than hoard cash for legal risk.

Second, the Supreme Court decision reasserts legal constraints on unilateral tariff power. Three reasons: one, it signals that trade policy cannot be used as a purely discretionary executive weapon; two, it forces future tariffs through narrower legal channels and greater scrutiny; three, that predictability reduces the risk premium on U.S. trade and manufacturing decisions.

Third, the rollback improves welfare even if some domestic producers lose protection. This matters because (1) tariffs act as a regressive consumption tax that disproportionately hurts lower-income households, (2) they raise costs for downstream U.S. manufacturers that rely on imported components, and (3) the net gain from cheaper inputs and lower consumer prices is larger than the concentrated benefit to protected industries.

prop_args.thesis: The refund process and tariff reversal create a strong deterrent against future protectionist overreach by making the fiscal and political costs visible.
mechanisms: First, the scale of the refunds exposes how expensive arbitrary tariff policy is. One, $35.5 billion is large enough to matter to the federal budget and to corporate balance sheets; two, it creates a public record of harm that opponents can cite; three, it makes future tariff threats less credible because markets now know they can be reversed in court.

Second, the ruling disciplines policymaking by shifting disputes into institutions rather than ad hoc executive action. Three reasons: one, firms can plan around stable rules; two, Congress and courts regain leverage over trade policy; three, allies and trading partners are less likely to retaliate preemptively when they expect legal constraints to hold.

Third, this reduces the chance of a self-reinforcing trade spiral. This matters because (1) if tariffs are easier to challenge, the administration has less room to escalate, (2) fewer retaliatory measures means less damage to exporters, and (3) the economy avoids the deadweight loss and uncertainty that usually accompany tariff wars.

opp_args.thesis: The refund ruling undermines U.S. industrial policy and weakens the government's ability to defend strategic sectors against foreign competition.
mechanisms: First, removing tariffs can expose vulnerable domestic industries to import competition before they are ready. One, sectors like steel, manufacturing, and politically sensitive supply chains often rely on temporary protection to survive; two, once capacity is lost it is costly and slow to rebuild; three, the U.S. may become more dependent on foreign suppliers in strategically important goods.

Second, the refund payout and legal defeat reduce deterrence against future trade abuse by foreign firms and states. One, if trading partners know U.S. tariffs can be struck down, they may test the limits of market access; two, domestic firms lose a bargaining chip in negotiations; three, the government becomes less able to use tariffs as leverage in broader security or industrial policy disputes.

Third, the administration's response shows the ruling may not end protectionism but simply shift it into more chaotic forms. One, Trump immediately pledged a 10% global tariff and new investigations, so the practical effect may be more uncertainty rather than less; two, firms face a moving target as policy oscillates between courts and executive retaliation; three, that instability can be worse than a consistent tariff regime because it discourages long-term investment.

opp_args.thesis: Even if tariffs are economically inefficient, they can be politically necessary to preserve domestic support for globalization and prevent deindustrialization backlash.
mechanisms: First, tariffs can function as compensation for communities harmed by trade shocks. One, import competition concentrates losses in specific regions and sectors; two, those workers often do not benefit immediately from lower consumer prices; three, visible protection can buy time for adjustment and reduce anti-trade populism.

Second, the refund and rollback may intensify political polarization over trade rather than settle it. One, businesses that benefited from protection will lobby for new barriers; two, workers in protected sectors may see the court as siding with elites and foreign competitors; three, that can fuel more extreme policy swings in future administrations.

Third, the case may strengthen the argument for more flexible executive trade tools. One, global supply chains move quickly and legislative processes are slow; two, presidents need rapid-response instruments for national security and bargaining; three, stripping those tools entirely may leave the U.S. less able to respond to unfair trade practices.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is between short-run price relief and long-run strategic autonomy. Prop wins if the judge prioritizes rule-of-law, lower consumer costs, and reduced uncertainty; Opp wins if they can show that tariff removal meaningfully weakens industrial capacity and leaves the U.S. less able to respond to strategic competition.
motion_areas: TH, as the United States, would sharply limit presidential tariff powers
THBT courts should strike down unilateral tariffs imposed without congressional approval
THP a world where tariff refunds are automatically issued after unlawful trade barriers are removed
THBT developing economies should resist using tariffs as a primary industrial policy tool

cards.title: Baltimore Bridge Collapse Charges Turn Maritime Safety Into a Corporate Criminal Liability Test
cards.background: Federal prosecutors in the United States have charged Synergy Marine, the operator of the cargo ship Dali, and one employee with conspiracy, obstruction and misconduct resulting in death after the ship struck Baltimore’s Francis Scott Key Bridge on 26 March 2024. The collapse killed six construction workers, halted shipping through the port, and left the city facing a reconstruction bill expected to take years and cost billions of dollars. Prosecutors allege the vessel lost power twice in four minutes because of a loose wire and improper fuel-pump use, and that Synergy hid safety problems from the US Coast Guard. In parallel, Maryland announced a $2.25bn civil settlement with Synergy, while the company has already paid more than $100m to the US Justice Department and $350m to Maryland’s insurer in related civil claims.

prop_args.thesis: Aggressive criminal and civil liability is necessary to force global shipping firms to internalize safety risks that otherwise get dumped onto workers, cities, and taxpayers.
mechanisms: First, punishment changes incentives in an industry where cost-cutting is structurally rewarded. This is because (1) ship operators face strong pressure to minimize maintenance and downtime, (2) the harms of failure are externalized onto ports, bridge authorities, and local governments, and (3) only large, credible penalties make it rational to invest in redundant safety systems and honest reporting.

Second, prosecution deters concealment and regulatory gaming. Three reasons: one, the indictment alleges Synergy knew about improper flushing-pump use and hid it; two, if firms can lie to investigators and still treat disasters as ordinary business losses, compliance becomes optional; three, criminal exposure creates personal and corporate consequences that civil settlements alone often do not.

Third, accountability protects public trust in maritime trade and infrastructure. This matters because the collapse killed six people, shut down a major shipping corridor, and imposed billions in losses; if the state does not visibly punish negligence, communities will see global commerce as a system that privatizes profits while socializing catastrophic risk.

opp_args.thesis: Over-criminalizing a complex industrial accident risks punishing a single operator for systemic failures that should be addressed through regulation, not headline-grabbing prosecutions.
mechanisms: First, maritime disasters usually arise from layered technical and institutional failures, not one bad actor. One, the NTSB identified multiple factors including a faulty cable, a fuel-pump problem, and bridge vulnerability; two, that means liability is diffuse across ship design, maintenance, inspection, and infrastructure standards; three, criminal charges can oversimplify causation and create bad precedent for future accidents.

Second, heavy-handed liability can distort incentives in the wrong direction. One, firms may become more defensive and less transparent with investigators if every disclosure risks prosecution; two, insurers and operators may pass costs onto trade and consumers, raising shipping prices; three, smaller operators may exit the market, reducing competition without necessarily improving safety.

Third, civil remedies and targeted safety reform may be more effective than criminal punishment. One, the state has already secured a $2.25bn settlement plus other payments, which directly funds reconstruction and compensation; two, regulators can mandate technical fixes and inspections more precisely than courts can; three, focusing on punishment may satisfy public anger without solving the underlying infrastructure and compliance failures.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether deterrence requires criminalization or whether the same safety gains can be achieved through regulation and civil liability. Prop has the stronger structural story if the round is about externalities and corporate impunity; opp is stronger if they can show causation is diffuse and that over-penalization chills cooperation and trade.
motion_areas: TH, as the US government, would prioritize criminal prosecution of corporations after catastrophic industrial accidents
THBT governments should impose criminal liability on shipping companies for preventable infrastructure disasters
THP a world where major transport accidents are treated primarily as corporate crimes rather than civil torts

cards.title: Israeli Report on 7 October Sexual Violence Hardens the Case for Hamas as a War-Crimes Actor
cards.background: An independent Israeli Civil Commission published a 300-page report on 12 May 2026 alleging that Hamas and other Palestinian armed groups used sexual violence systematically during the 7 October 2023 attacks. The report draws on 430 filmed interviews, more than 10,000 photographs and videos, and official records; it says sexual violence was used to “maximize pain and suffering” and continued against hostages in captivity. The attacks killed about 1,200 people and saw 251 taken hostage; the report says the crimes constitute war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocidal acts under international law.

prop_args.thesis: This report strengthens the case that Hamas is not a conventional resistance movement but an actor willing to use atrocity crimes as a deliberate tool of war, which should radically narrow its legitimacy and diplomatic space.
mechanisms: First, it reframes Hamas’s violence as strategic terror rather than battlefield excess. This is because (1) the report alleges sexual violence was systematic and intended to maximize suffering, (2) the abuse extended beyond the initial attack into hostage captivity, and (3) the targeting of family members and civilians shows coercion aimed at social breakdown, not military advantage.

Second, it increases the credibility and durability of international legal and political pressure on Hamas. Three reasons: one, a 300-page independent archive with 430 interviews and 10,000+ images/videos is harder to dismiss than isolated testimony; two, the report explicitly maps conduct onto war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocidal acts; three, preserved evidence can be used in future prosecutions, sanctions designations, and travel restrictions.

Third, it changes the conflict narrative in ways that matter for coalition-building and ceasefire politics. This matters because (1) states and publics are more willing to isolate groups associated with sexual violence than groups framed as insurgents, (2) it weakens sympathy-based diplomatic campaigns for Hamas, and (3) it gives Israel and its allies a stronger moral and legal basis to demand demilitarization or exclusion from post-war governance.

opp_args.thesis: The report will have limited practical effect because the conflict is already driven by entrenched military and political realities, and atrocity documentation does not by itself change Hamas’s incentives or the war’s trajectory.
mechanisms: First, legal condemnation does not equal operational leverage. 1) Hamas is not dependent on Western legitimacy in the way a state is, 2) its core incentives are survival, deterrence, and bargaining over hostages, and 3) groups under existential pressure often become more, not less, willing to absorb reputational costs.

Second, the report may be politically discounted because the information environment around the war is already heavily polarized. 1) The article notes that some early Israeli claims after 7 October were later found false, 2) that history makes audiences more skeptical of Israeli-linked investigations, and 3) competing narratives about Gaza’s civilian death toll will drown out legal findings in many global forums.

Third, even strong atrocity evidence can be strategically counterproductive if it hardens maximalist positions. 1) It can deepen Israeli public resolve against concessions, 2) it can reduce space for prisoner exchanges or ceasefire compromises by making compromise look like impunity, and 3) it can entrench a cycle where each side treats the other as beyond negotiation.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is between symbolic/legal delegitimation and actual battlefield or diplomatic change. Prop wins if the motion is about narrative, accountability, or post-conflict governance; opp wins if the question is immediate war termination, because atrocity findings alone do not alter Hamas’s coercive incentives or Israel’s military posture.
motion_areas: TH, as an international community, would prioritize atrocity documentation over immediate ceasefire diplomacy in conflicts involving non-state armed groups
THBT states should refuse political engagement with armed groups credibly accused of systematic sexual violence
THP a world where war crimes evidence can be preserved and used for future prosecutions even when immediate justice is impossible

cards.title: Warsh’s Fed Ascension Puts U.S. Monetary Policy Under a More Politicized Chair
cards.background: On Tuesday, the U.S. Senate confirmed Kevin Warsh to the Federal Reserve Board of Governors by a 51-45 vote, giving him a 14-year term on the central bank’s board. The Senate is expected to hold a separate vote later this week on whether to make him chair of the Federal Reserve, a four-year post that would succeed Jerome Powell. Bloomberg reports that the chair confirmation is likely to pass with similar margins.

prop_args.thesis: Confirming Warsh as Fed chair increases the risk of politicized monetary policy and weaker central bank credibility.
mechanisms: First, a chair chosen through a visibly partisan confirmation process weakens the Fed’s perceived independence. This is because (1) markets infer that future rate decisions may be more responsive to White House or Senate preferences, (2) inflation expectations become less anchored when the institution looks politically captured, and (3) even if policy does not immediately change, credibility losses raise the premium investors demand on U.S. assets.

Second, Warsh’s chairmanship can shift the Fed toward a more growth- or market-friendly bias at the expense of inflation control. Three reasons: one, a chair has agenda-setting power over meetings, communications, and consensus-building; two, the chair’s public signaling shapes market expectations more than any single governor; three, if the chair is seen as more dovish or politically aligned, the Fed may tolerate looser conditions for longer, increasing medium-term inflation risk.

Third, the structural harm is that a politicized Fed creates a bad precedent for future administrations. This matters because once the chair is treated as a partisan prize, each transition becomes a contest over monetary direction rather than technocratic stewardship, making long-run policy less stable and increasing volatility in rates, currency markets, and investment planning.

opp_args.thesis: Warsh’s confirmation is a normal personnel change that can improve Fed accountability without meaningfully undermining independence.
mechanisms: First, the Fed is institutionally insulated enough that one chair cannot single-handedly hijack policy. (1) The chair still needs majority support from the Board and FOMC, (2) the 14-year governor term outlasts any single administration, and (3) markets care more about actual inflation data and committee votes than about one appointment.

Second, a more skeptical or reform-minded chair can correct policy drift and improve performance. (1) If the Fed has been too slow to react to inflation or financial imbalances, a new chair can tighten communication and discipline, (2) leadership change can reduce groupthink inside the institution, and (3) clearer accountability can make the Fed more responsive to Congress and the public without eliminating operational independence.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether the chairmanship meaningfully changes the Fed’s behavior or just its optics. Prop wins if it can show that credibility and expectations are themselves core monetary tools; opp wins if it proves the committee structure and data dependence dominate any individual chair’s preferences.

THBT the Senate should not confirm central bank chairs through partisan votes
THP a world where central bank governors are appointed by bipartisan supermajorities

cards.title: Trump-Xi Beijing Summit Tests Whether Personal Diplomacy Can Reset U.S.-China Rivalry
cards.background: President Donald Trump is set to visit Beijing on Wednesday, becoming the first US leader to do so in almost a decade. The summit with President Xi Jinping was originally delayed from March because of the Iran war. The meeting is framed as a chance to reset personal ties and seek common ground on trade, technology, and other contentious issues between the world’s two largest economies.

prop_args.thesis: A high-level Trump-Xi summit can reduce escalation risk and create a narrow but valuable window for stabilizing the U.S.-China relationship.
mechanisms: First, direct leader-to-leader diplomacy lowers misperception and crisis risk. This is because (1) both sides can clarify red lines without bureaucratic distortion, (2) personal rapport can speed up de-escalation in moments of tension, and (3) summitry creates a visible commitment device that makes sudden policy shocks politically costlier.

Second, even limited agreements on trade and technology can produce immediate economic spillovers. Three reasons: one, firms on both sides gain more certainty about tariffs and export controls; two, reduced uncertainty encourages investment and supply-chain planning; three, a partial thaw can prevent tit-for-tat measures from broadening into a full economic decoupling.

Third, symbolic engagement matters because it preserves channels for future bargaining on bigger issues. This matters because a stable baseline of communication is often the difference between managed competition and accidental confrontation, especially when the two largest economies are also strategic rivals.

opp_args.thesis: The summit is more likely to entrench rivalry than resolve it, because the structural drivers of U.S.-China competition overwhelm any personal chemistry between Trump and Xi.
mechanisms: First, the meeting cannot solve the underlying security and technology conflict. One, both states see semiconductors, AI, and advanced manufacturing as core national-power assets; two, domestic political incentives reward toughness rather than compromise; three, any deal that looks like concession risks being reversed after the summit.

Second, summit diplomacy can create false optimism without changing behavior. One, leaders may issue vague statements to claim success while leaving tariffs, export controls, and military competition intact; two, markets may misread symbolism as substantive détente; three, the gap between rhetoric and policy can make future breakdowns more damaging.

Third, personal diplomacy can actually worsen bargaining dynamics. One, if Xi believes Trump values a headline deal, China can extract concessions while offering limited structural change; two, if Trump seeks a visible win, he may overstate progress and weaken U.S. leverage; three, the result is a fragile pause rather than durable stabilization.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether summitry can change structural incentives or merely paper over them. Prop wins if the round is about crisis management and short-term stability; opp wins if the clash is about durable great-power competition, because the underlying security dilemma and domestic politics give both sides strong reasons to revert.

cards.title: US Political and Commercial Pressure Risks Unravelling Bosnia’s Dayton Settlement
cards.region: Bosnia and Herzegovina / United States / Western Balkans
cards.background: The UN high representative for Bosnia and Herzegovina, Christian Schmidt, warned the UN Security Council that the country’s multi-ethnic constitutional order is under threat after a policy clash with the United States forced him to resign. The high representative post was created by the 1995 Dayton peace agreement, which ended a three-year war that killed more than 100,000 people, and gives wide powers to interpret and amend laws. Schmidt has spent five years in office and has repeatedly clashed with Republika Srpska’s former president Milorad Dodik, whose US sanctions were lifted last year in a move not coordinated with the EU.

prop_args.thesis: US interference in Bosnia weakens the Dayton settlement by empowering secessionists and removing the only external actor capable of enforcing constitutional order.
mechanisms: First, it removes enforcement capacity. This is because (1) the high representative is the only actor with authority to override local obstruction and protect state institutions, (2) Bosnia’s two-entity system already incentivises paralysis, and (3) without credible external enforcement, Republika Srpska can ignore constitutional court rulings and state-level decisions with fewer costs.

Second, it signals to Dodik and other secessionists that the US is no longer committed to Bosnia’s territorial integrity. Three reasons: one, sanctions were lifted on Dodik despite continued secessionist rhetoric; two, the US appears willing to bargain over the post itself; three, commercial actors linked to Trump allies are openly pursuing deals in Republika Srpska, which normalises engagement with anti-state forces.

Third, this creates a precedent that great-power patronage can override peace architecture. This matters because (1) it encourages local elites to seek foreign sponsors instead of compromise, (2) it makes EU and UN guarantees look reversible, and (3) it raises the risk of renewed constitutional crisis or eventual partition, which is far harder to reverse than short-term instability.

opp_args.thesis: Reducing the high representative’s role and allowing a more transactional US approach could improve Bosnia’s stability by lowering nationalist backlash and forcing domestic compromise.
mechanisms: First, the high representative can itself be a source of legitimacy problems. one, Dodik and Republika Srpska already reject Schmidt as lacking legitimacy; two, heavy-handed external intervention lets secessionists frame themselves as defenders of sovereignty; three, removing or weakening the post may deprive them of a rallying cry and reduce mobilisation around anti-state politics.

Second, US commercial engagement can substitute for coercion by creating material incentives for cooperation. one, energy and infrastructure investment can bind Republika Srpska and the Federation into shared economic interests; two, dependence on US-backed LNG infrastructure may reduce reliance on Russian energy and weaken Moscow-linked patronage; three, development gains can make secession economically less attractive than remaining in a functioning state.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether external pressure is a stabilising guarantor or a delegitimising trigger. Prop wins if the round is about preventing state collapse, because Bosnia’s institutions are structurally fragile and the loss of enforcement power creates immediate security risk; Opp only wins if they prove that the old intervention model was already unsustainable and that transactional investment can credibly replace it.

THBT international guarantors should retain coercive powers in fragile peace settlements
THP a world where the Dayton framework is replaced by domestic sovereignty in Bosnia and Herzegovina
THBT the West should sanction secessionist leaders even at the cost of short-term diplomatic friction

cards.title: South Africa’s Asylum Clampdown Prioritizes Deportability Over Refugee Reassessment
cards.background: South Africa’s Constitutional Court has ruled that foreign nationals cannot reapply for asylum after a rejection, overturning a Supreme Court of Appeal decision in a case brought by two Burundian nationals. The court said unlimited repeat applications could create a "never-ending cycle" that blocks deportations and causes administrative chaos. South Africa hosts more than 167,000 refugees and asylum seekers in 2025, mainly from Burundi, the DRC, Somalia, South Sudan, Rwanda and Zimbabwe, while the country is also facing protests and violence targeting undocumented migrants.

prop_args.thesis: Limiting repeat asylum claims is necessary to preserve the integrity and enforceability of South Africa’s refugee system.
mechanisms: First, it stops strategic delay tactics that turn asylum into a de facto stay permit. This is because (1) repeated applications can be used to prolong legal presence after a first rejection, (2) that makes deportation functionally impossible even where claims have already been assessed, and (3) the state loses any credible enforcement mechanism, which incentivizes more non-meritorious claims.

Second, it reduces administrative overload and restores capacity to process genuine cases. Three reasons: one, asylum systems have finite staff, courts, and appeal capacity; two, repeat filings force officials to relitigate the same person instead of clearing backlogs; three, backlogs punish real refugees by delaying protection and work access for everyone else.

Third, it strengthens public legitimacy for refugee protection by separating genuine asylum from abuse. This matters because (1) South Africa is already facing anti-migrant protests and demands for mass deportations, (2) visible loopholes feed the perception that the system is being gamed, and (3) a tighter process makes it easier for the government to defend refugee protection politically against xenophobic backlash.

opp_args.thesis: Barring repeat applications risks returning people to danger when conditions in their home country materially change after an initial rejection.
mechanisms: First, asylum claims are time-sensitive and country conditions can deteriorate rapidly. One, Burundi experienced major political violence after the 2015 presidential election, including at least 70 deaths; two, a person rejected in 2014 may face a genuinely different risk profile in 2018 or later; three, a blanket bar treats a stale decision as permanently accurate even when facts change.

Second, the ruling creates a procedural trap for people who lacked a fair or complete first hearing. One, asylum seekers often have weak legal representation, language barriers, or missing documentation; two, a first rejection may reflect evidentiary failure rather than lack of persecution; three, denying any reapplication removes a safety valve for correcting wrongful decisions and increases refoulement risk.

Third, the policy externalizes burden onto neighboring states and informal survival strategies. One, if people cannot regularize status after conditions worsen, they are pushed into illegality, exploitation, and underground work; two, that makes monitoring and integration harder for the state; three, it can also drive secondary movement to other countries, spreading regional instability rather than solving it.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is between administrative control and non-refoulement. Prop wins if the core issue is system abuse and state capacity; opp wins if the core issue is whether a rigid procedural bar can safely track changing persecution risks in a volatile region.
motion_areas: TH, as South Africa, would bar repeat asylum applications after a final rejection
THBT states should not allow unlimited reapplication for asylum absent materially new evidence
THP a world where asylum systems prioritize finality over repeated review

cards.title: UAE’s covert strike on Iran risks turning Gulf hedging into open regional war
cards.region: United Arab Emirates / Iran / Kuwait / Gulf states
cards.background: Reporting says the UAE secretly launched a major retaliatory attack on Iran during the recent conflict, including a strike on Iran’s Lazan Island just before the 7 April ceasefire. Kuwait separately said at least four IRGC members were captured trying to carry out attacks on Bubiyan Island, while Iran had already targeted UAE facilities earlier in the fighting that began on 28 February. The UAE’s biggest gas plant has reportedly been disrupted by Iranian attacks, with Adnoc Gas saying full repair will not be completed until 2027. The US has also signaled continued support for Gulf defenses, including Iron Dome batteries and personnel sent to the UAE.

prop_args.thesis: The UAE’s covert retaliation is strategically necessary because it deters Iranian coercion and prevents Gulf states from becoming passive targets in a widening shadow war.
mechanisms: First, it raises the expected cost of Iranian escalation. This is because (1) Iran can no longer assume Gulf states will only absorb strikes and rely on US protection, (2) covert retaliation creates uncertainty over where and how the next response will come from, and (3) that uncertainty forces Tehran to spend more on defense, dispersion, and counterintelligence.

Second, it restores deterrence credibility for smaller Gulf states. Three reasons: one, if the UAE does not respond after repeated missile and drone attacks, Iran learns that coercion works; two, visible passivity would invite further strikes on oil, ports, and gas infrastructure; three, retaliation signals to Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, and Qatar that Gulf sovereignty is not cost-free to violate.

Third, it protects the broader regional balance by preventing Iran from monopolizing escalation. This matters because (1) if only Iran can strike while others abstain, Tehran controls the tempo of conflict, (2) limited Gulf reprisals can be calibrated below the threshold of all-out war, and (3) a credible counter-threat may actually help preserve the ceasefire by making renewed attacks less attractive.

opp_args.thesis: The UAE’s secret attack is reckless because it increases the probability of a direct interstate war that Gulf states are structurally unable to sustain.
mechanisms: First, it collapses the ambiguity that previously insulated Gulf states from becoming formal belligerents. One, once Iran has evidence that the UAE is not neutral, UAE territory becomes a legitimate target in Tehran’s eyes; two, that expands the target set from military assets to oil, desalination, shipping, and civilian infrastructure; three, it makes de-escalation politically harder because each side must now save face after a direct exchange.

Second, it triggers asymmetric Iranian retaliation that Gulf states cannot absorb. One, Iran can hit ports, gas plants, and shipping lanes far more cheaply than the Gulf can defend them; two, the UAE and Saudi Arabia depend on vulnerable coastal infrastructure and the Strait of Hormuz; three, even limited disruption can create massive economic and humanitarian damage, as shown by the near two-year closure of the UAE’s biggest gas plant.

Third, it fractures Gulf unity and undermines the very coalition needed to manage Iran. One, Saudi Arabia prefers restraint while the UAE appears more hawkish, so the attack deepens intra-Gulf splits; two, Kuwait’s reported IRGC infiltration shows that even neutral states are now being pulled in; three, once each Gulf state fears being singled out, they hedge individually rather than coordinate collectively, which weakens deterrence and increases the chance of miscalculation.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether retaliation restores deterrence or converts a shadow conflict into an overt regional war. Prop wins if you believe limited covert force can raise costs without crossing the threshold of all-out escalation; opp wins if you think Gulf infrastructure is too exposed and Iran’s retaliation capacity is too asymmetric for that gamble to be safe.

THBT Gulf states should respond militarily to Iranian attacks rather than rely on US protection
THP a world where middle powers can conduct limited covert reprisals without public attribution
THBT Gulf monarchies should prioritize deterrence over diplomatic restraint in dealing with Iran

cards.title: Israel’s War Turns Lebanon’s Education Collapse Into a Long-Term Sectarian and Class Divide
cards.background: Israel intensified its war on Lebanon on March 2, 2026, after months of attacks and more than 10,000 reported violations of the November 2024 ceasefire, according to the article. Since then, more than 1.2 million people in Lebanon have been displaced, including 500,000 school-aged children, while UNESCO says 339 schools are in warzones, hundreds more are being used as shelters, and another 100 schools are in high-risk areas. Lebanon’s education system was already under severe strain from the 2019 economic crisis, COVID-19, and currency collapse; teachers’ salaries have fallen by about 80% in real terms and around 30% of the sector has left the country or changed professions since 2019.

prop_args.thesis: Israel’s war is not just causing immediate humanitarian harm; it is entrenching a generational education gap that will deepen Lebanon’s instability and weaken national cohesion for years.
mechanisms: First, the war destroys the basic conditions for schooling, so learning loss becomes cumulative rather than temporary. This is because (1) 339 schools are in warzones and hundreds more are shelters, so physical access is gone; (2) 500,000 school-aged children have been displaced, so attendance is interrupted across entire communities; (3) repeated disruption since 2019 means students have already lost multiple years, making catch-up increasingly unrealistic.

Second, the crisis widens class inequality because only wealthier families can absorb the costs of continuity. Three reasons: one, online or hybrid learning requires internet, electricity, and devices that poor households often lack; two, families must choose between food, transport, heating, and education, so poorer children drop out first; three, those who fall out of school are more exposed to child labour and child marriage, locking in poverty across generations.

Third, the war undermines Lebanon’s civic fabric by turning education into a survival system rather than a nation-building institution. This matters because (1) schools are where shared civic identity is built in a sectarian society; (2) when citizenship and social studies are dropped in favor of math and science recovery, students lose the common framework that reduces sectarian fragmentation; (3) trauma, displacement, and isolation create a cohort less likely to trust institutions or participate in stable politics.

opp_args.thesis: The education crisis is real, but the war is exposing pre-existing state failure rather than creating a uniquely new lost generation, so the blame and policy focus should stay on Lebanon’s broken institutions.
mechanisms: First, Lebanon’s education system was already collapsing before the current escalation. One, the country had been in economic crisis since 2019; two, the Gini coefficient rose from 0.32 in 2011 to 0.61 in 2023, showing extreme inequality; three, teachers’ salaries had already fallen by about 80%, and 30% of the sector had left, so war is accelerating a pre-existing decline rather than being the root cause.

Second, the system still has adaptive capacity, so the outcome is not necessarily a permanent lost generation. One, schools and the Ministry are using online learning, multiple shifts, temporary learning centres, and psychosocial services; two, UNESCO and NGOs are coordinating support, meaning there is an external safety net; three, prioritizing core subjects like math and science can preserve human capital even during conflict, limiting long-term scarring.

Third, the strongest long-term determinant is post-war reconstruction, not the war itself. One, if ceasefire and aid stabilize access, children can re-enter school and recover lost years; two, the real bottleneck is funding and governance, since humanitarian support is under strain and corruption is endemic; three, blaming the war alone risks obscuring the domestic reforms needed to fix Lebanon’s education system.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether the war creates irreversible scarring or merely intensifies an already fragile system. Prop wins if it proves that displacement, school destruction, and teacher flight convert temporary interruption into permanent inequality; Opp wins if it shows Lebanon’s pre-existing collapse and available stop-gap measures mean the long-term outcome depends more on governance and reconstruction than on the war itself.

THBT post-conflict reconstruction should focus first on restoring schools and teachers before large-scale infrastructure projects
THP a world where wartime education is delivered primarily through remote and temporary learning systems
THBT states in civil or interstate conflict should be held internationally responsible for educational destruction

cards.title: US-EU Trade Frictions Become a Growth Drag and Strategic Liability
cards.background: At JPMorgan Chase’s annual Global Markets Conference in Paris on 12 May 2026, CEO Jamie Dimon said the US and Europe need to fix “stupid” trade issues to improve growth. In the same interview, he argued the US would also benefit from a stronger NATO. The article is a short Bloomberg video summary and does not specify the exact trade disputes he was referring to.

prop_args.thesis: Reducing US-EU trade frictions is a pro-growth move because it lowers costs, restores investment confidence, and strengthens the transatlantic economic bloc against external shocks.
mechanisms: First, lower trade barriers increase efficiency and reduce input costs. This is because (1) firms on both sides can source from the cheapest/most productive suppliers, (2) supply chains become less fragmented and less exposed to tariff-induced price spikes, and (3) consumers face lower prices, which supports demand and real incomes.

Second, resolving trade disputes improves business certainty and capital allocation. Three reasons: one, companies are more willing to commit to long-horizon investment when market access is predictable; two, fewer regulatory and tariff disputes reduce compliance and legal costs; three, cross-border mergers, joint ventures, and industrial partnerships become easier to structure.

Third, a more integrated US-EU economic relationship has strategic spillovers. This matters because a cohesive transatlantic market can coordinate standards, reduce dependence on rival blocs, and create a larger demand base that cushions both economies during global downturns.

opp_args.thesis: Trade frictions are not the main constraint on growth, and fixing them may produce limited gains while exposing domestic industries and workers to political backlash.
mechanisms: First, the growth payoff may be modest because the biggest drivers of US and European performance are domestic productivity, monetary conditions, energy prices, and labor-market constraints, not headline trade disputes. One, if the core problem is weak investment or high rates, trade liberalization does little; two, if firms already trade heavily under existing rules, the marginal gain from further fixes is smaller; three, governments may overestimate trade as a cure-all and neglect deeper structural reforms.

Second, reducing trade barriers can create concentrated losses that outweigh diffuse gains politically. One, import-competing sectors face sharper competition and may cut jobs or wages; two, governments then face pressure to reintroduce protection or subsidies, undermining the reform; three, backlash can fuel populism and make future cooperation harder, especially in sensitive sectors like steel, autos, and digital services.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether trade liberalization is a meaningful growth lever or just a marginal adjustment relative to domestic macro and productivity constraints. Prop wins if the round is about long-run efficiency and strategic bloc-building; opp wins if the judge prioritizes political feasibility and the limited size of the economic gain.
motion_areas: TH, as the US, would prioritize resolving trade disputes with Europe over new protectionist measures
THBT the US and EU should deepen economic integration despite domestic political backlash
THP a world where transatlantic trade barriers are significantly reduced

cards.title: Kuwait’s Foiled IRGC Infiltration Turns Gulf Maritime Security Into an Open Iran-Kuwait Confrontation
cards.background: Kuwait says it arrested four men it identified as members of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) after they allegedly tried to infiltrate Bubiyan Island by sea on May 1 and injured a Kuwaiti soldier in the confrontation. Kuwait’s Interior Ministry said the men were aboard a fishing boat chartered to carry out hostile actions and that two other suspects escaped. Bubiyan is Kuwait’s largest island, near key shipping lanes, northern oilfields, and military installations; Kuwait also said it recently intercepted hostile drones and previously blamed Iran for strikes on the Mina al-Ahmadi refinery and a power/desalination plant.

prop_args.thesis: Publicly attributing and punishing the IRGC incursion is necessary to deter further Iranian gray-zone attacks and defend Kuwait’s sovereignty.
mechanisms: First, a visible response raises the expected cost of future infiltration attempts. This is because (1) covert maritime raids depend on ambiguity and low attribution, (2) naming the IRGC and summoning Iran’s ambassador reduces deniability, and (3) signaling Article 51 self-defence tells Tehran that small-scale probes can escalate into a broader state response.

Second, Kuwait must harden the norm that attacks on islands, ports, and energy infrastructure are not tolerable. Three reasons: one, Bubiyan sits near strategic shipping lanes and military sites, so failure to respond invites repeat targeting; two, the region already saw alleged drone and refinery attacks, so silence would normalize escalation; three, Gulf states coordinate through precedent, so Kuwait’s response helps create a collective red line.

Third, the move protects domestic confidence in the state’s ability to secure water, energy, and trade infrastructure. This matters because Kuwait is only about 80km from Iran’s coast and is highly dependent on desalination, so even limited attacks can create panic, insurance shocks, and pressure on the government to overreact later.

opp_args.thesis: Escalating the incident publicly risks feeding a security spiral that makes Kuwait less safe and more vulnerable to retaliation.
mechanisms: First, attribution and retaliation can provoke asymmetric Iranian responses. One, Iran can deny direct involvement and use proxies or cyber tools instead of conventional force; two, public humiliation increases incentives to retaliate to restore deterrence; three, Kuwait’s small size and proximity to Iran make it hard to absorb repeated low-level attacks.

Second, the incident may be better handled through quiet diplomacy and intelligence cooperation than maximalist confrontation. One, the article says there was no immediate Iranian reaction, so there is still space for de-escalation; two, public escalation can close off backchannels that are essential in Gulf crisis management; three, Kuwait depends on stable maritime routes and energy flows, so a tit-for-tat cycle would impose immediate economic costs.

Third, over-attributing every attack to Iran can entrench miscalculation and reduce credibility if evidence is incomplete. One, Kuwait has already blamed Iran for earlier refinery and plant strikes, so repeating the claim without transparent proof can look politically motivated; two, if later evidence is weaker than the accusation, Kuwait’s deterrent messaging loses force; three, in a region with multiple armed actors, misattribution can widen the conflict beyond the original incident.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether deterrence or escalation risk dominates. Prop wins if the judge prioritizes sovereignty and the need to stop repeated gray-zone attacks; opp wins if they think Kuwait’s small geographic exposure makes any public confrontation disproportionately dangerous and better handled through covert diplomacy.

THBT small states should respond forcefully to gray-zone attacks rather than rely on quiet diplomacy
THP a world where Gulf states treat maritime infiltration as an act of war

cards.title: Microsoft’s Israel Unit Exposes the Corporate Risk of Enabling Military Mass Surveillance
cards.background: Microsoft’s head of its Israeli subsidiary, Alon Haimovich, is stepping down after an internal inquiry into the company’s dealings with the Israeli military. The inquiry followed a Guardian/+972 Magazine/Local Call investigation that found Unit 8200 used Microsoft’s Azure cloud to store a vast archive of intercepted Palestinian phone calls from Gaza and the West Bank. Microsoft said it found Unit 8200 had violated its terms of service, which prohibit mass surveillance, and cut off the unit’s access to cloud and AI products used for the project.

prop_args.thesis: Multinational tech firms should be held accountable when their infrastructure is used for state mass surveillance, because commercial neutrality becomes complicity once they knowingly enable abuse.
mechanisms: First, enforcement of corporate ethics matters because (1) cloud providers are not passive carriers but active enablers with control over storage, compute, and access, (2) once a firm supplies the architecture for surveillance it lowers the cost and scale of abuse, and (3) terminating access creates a real deterrent for other clients and subsidiaries that might hide end-use from headquarters.

Second, this case shows why internal compliance and transparency are essential. Three reasons: one, local managers can have incentives to maximize revenue and understate risk; two, without independent inquiry headquarters cannot verify whether products are being used for mass rights violations; three, public exposure forces firms to align sales with stated policies, preserving the credibility of their own codes of conduct.

Third, cutting off abusive military use protects civilians and the company’s long-term legitimacy. This matters because (1) mass surveillance chills speech and movement for millions of Palestinians, (2) reputational damage can trigger employee backlash, investor scrutiny, and regulatory action across other markets, and (3) a hard line against surveillance preserves trust in cloud and AI products, which is essential for business growth.

opp_args.thesis: Punishing a subsidiary over military contracts risks overcorrecting in a way that politicizes business, weakens local operations, and may not meaningfully change state surveillance behavior.
mechanisms: First, the commercial and operational costs can be severe: (1) cutting ties with a major government client can reduce revenue and local market access, (2) it may encourage other states to view the firm as unreliable in sensitive sectors, and (3) it can push the company to retreat from regions where its services are most needed for ordinary business and public infrastructure.

Second, the policy may have limited impact on the underlying abuse. Three sub-reasons: one, states with strong security imperatives can shift to domestic vendors or other foreign providers; two, surveillance programs are often embedded in intelligence doctrine, so losing one supplier does not end the practice; three, public corporate sanctions can harden the state’s resolve by framing the issue as external interference rather than rights compliance.

Third, overbroad corporate policing creates governance problems. One, headquarters may lack the expertise to judge intelligence use cases in conflict zones; two, firms may become risk-averse and refuse legitimate security or public-sector contracts; three, a precedent of retroactive punishment can chill investment in politically sensitive markets and make global tech fragmentation worse.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether corporate withdrawal meaningfully constrains abusive surveillance or simply imposes costs on the firm while the state adapts. Prop wins if the round is about accountability and civilian harm; opp wins if the round emphasizes limited leverage, substitution, and the risk of politicizing global business.
motion_areas: TH, as a multinational tech company, would refuse all contracts that enable state surveillance
THBT tech firms should be legally liable for the end-use of their cloud infrastructure in human rights abuses
THP a world where cloud providers can unilaterally cut off government clients for rights violations
TH, as a Western corporation, would prioritize human rights compliance over market expansion in conflict zones

cards.title: Ukraine’s Anti-Corruption Crackdown Risks Weakening Zelensky’s Wartime Coalition and EU Accession Bid
cards.background: Andriy Yermak, Volodymyr Zelensky’s former chief of staff and long-time close adviser, appeared in a Kyiv court after Ukraine’s anti-corruption agencies named him a suspect in a money-laundering case. The case is part of a broader probe by SAPO and NABU into an alleged $100m embezzlement scheme in Ukraine’s nuclear energy sector, alongside a separate $10.5m luxury housing project outside Kyiv called “Dynasty.” The scandal has already implicated or touched several figures in Zelensky’s circle, including ex-Deputy Prime Minister Oleksiy Chernyshov, businessman Timur Mindich, and ex-Energy Minister Herman Haluschenko. The allegations come after Zelensky previously had to scrap a law that weakened anti-corruption agencies following protests and EU criticism, and as Ukraine continues to pursue EU membership during Russia’s full-scale invasion.

prop_args.thesis: A serious anti-corruption crackdown strengthens Ukraine in the long run by preserving state legitimacy, unlocking EU integration, and improving wartime governance.
mechanisms: First, it restores domestic and international trust in the Ukrainian state. This is because (1) wartime societies tolerate sacrifice only if they believe elites are being held to the same standards, (2) visible prosecutions reduce the perception that aid and reconstruction money are being stolen, and (3) cleaner institutions make it easier for Zelensky to keep public support despite battlefield losses.

Second, it materially improves Ukraine’s EU accession prospects. Three reasons: one, the EU has repeatedly tied enlargement to judicial independence and anti-corruption enforcement; two, the fact that Zelensky already had to reverse a law weakening NABU and SAPO shows Brussels is watching institutional backsliding closely; three, prosecuting even insiders signals that Ukraine is converging with EU governance norms rather than entrenching oligarchic capture.

Third, it improves military and economic effectiveness by reducing leakage. This matters because corruption in the nuclear and construction sectors is not abstract: (1) it diverts scarce wartime funds, (2) it weakens procurement and energy resilience, and (3) it creates a cleaner environment for donor states and private investors to continue financing Ukraine’s defense and reconstruction.

opp_args.thesis: The scandal weakens Ukraine because aggressive anti-corruption action during wartime fractures the ruling coalition, distracts leadership, and risks destabilizing the state at the exact moment it needs unity.
mechanisms: First, it creates elite fragmentation and governance paralysis. One, Yermak was Zelensky’s closest adviser and led talks with the US, so removing him disrupts foreign policy coordination; two, repeated raids and resignations signal that the president’s inner circle is under siege, making officials more risk-averse and less effective; three, when key personnel are consumed by legal defense, they cannot focus on war management.

Second, it can be politically weaponized and erode wartime morale. One, corruption probes against top insiders can be framed by opponents as proof that the entire government is rotten; two, public scandal during wartime can reduce trust in mobilization, taxation, and sacrifice; three, if citizens believe aid is being siphoned off, support for continued resistance and reforms can collapse.

Third, it may slow EU and donor coordination in practice even if it helps on paper. One, leadership turnover and institutional infighting create uncertainty for Brussels and Washington; two, donors may delay disbursements while waiting for clearer control over corruption risks; three, a state fighting both Russia and internal purges has less bandwidth to negotiate security guarantees, weapons deliveries, and accession benchmarks.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether accountability strengthens resilience or whether wartime instability overwhelms reform gains. Prop wins if the round is about long-run state capacity and EU integration; Opp wins if the round prioritizes immediate wartime cohesion and the risk that elite scandal undermines command, morale, and donor confidence.
motion_areas: TH, as Ukraine, would aggressively prosecute corruption even during wartime
THBT wartime governments should prioritize anti-corruption enforcement over elite cohesion
THP a world where EU accession is conditioned on prosecuting senior wartime officials

cards.title: US-Iran War Costs Expose the Tradeoff Between Middle East Escalation and Great-Power Deterrence
cards.region: United States / Iran / Israel / Middle East
cards.background: The Pentagon told a Senate committee on 12 May 2026 that the US-Israel war with Iran has cost the United States $29bn, up from the $25bn figure it disclosed in late April. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the administration is prepared to both escalate and de-escalate, while President Trump rejected a new Iranian ceasefire proposal and described the pause in fighting as "on life support." The article says fighting has been generally paused since 8 April, but the administration has not disclosed the full damage to US installations or the extent of munitions depletion.

prop_args.thesis: The war is an economically irrational commitment that drains US fiscal capacity, raises inflationary pressure, and weakens America’s broader strategic posture.
mechanisms: First, the conflict imposes direct budgetary costs that crowd out other spending. This is because (1) the Pentagon has already revised the bill upward from $25bn to $29bn in less than a month, (2) the department is asking Congress for a historic $1.5tn funding request, and (3) every additional dollar spent on Iran is a dollar not available for readiness, domestic priorities, or Indo-Pacific deterrence.

Second, the war feeds domestic inflation and political backlash. Three reasons: one, the article links the conflict to rising gasoline prices, with US petrol prices up 5.4 percent in April; two, CPI inflation was 3.8 percent year-on-year, the highest since 2023; three, higher energy prices and war spending together make the administration look economically incompetent, which is especially dangerous ahead of the November midterms.

Third, the conflict creates strategic overextension by forcing the US to split attention between Iran and China. This matters because the Joint Chiefs explicitly say China remains the top priority, yet the Pentagon must simultaneously manage escalation in the Strait of Hormuz, repair damaged assets, and replenish munitions, meaning the US pays more to get less deterrence in the theater that matters most long-term.

opp_args.thesis: The war is a necessary strategic investment because failing to confront Iran would be costlier in the long run and would undermine US deterrence globally.
mechanisms: First, the spending prevents a larger regional security shock. One, if Iran is allowed to absorb pressure without response, it can close or threaten the Strait of Hormuz and impose far bigger oil and shipping costs on the global economy; two, a limited war today may avert a wider war later; three, visible US commitment reassures Israel and Gulf partners that deterrence still works.

Second, the munitions and cost concerns are manageable and should not dictate strategy. One, Hegseth claims the Pentagon knows its stockpiles and has "plenty" of what it needs; two, the US defense budget is large enough to absorb a $29bn contingency without structural collapse; three, temporary depletion is preferable to allowing an adversary to learn that America will not spend resources to defend core interests.

Third, backing down would damage credibility more than the war damages the budget. One, if the US pauses under pressure, Iran and other rivals infer that American threats are hollow; two, deterrence failures invite future challenges in the Middle East and beyond; three, the reputational cost of inaction can be more expensive than the immediate fiscal outlay.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is between short-term fiscal pain and long-term strategic credibility. Prop wins if you prioritize concrete economic harm and domestic political backlash; opp wins if you think the marginal cost of escalation is smaller than the cost of letting Iran rewrite the regional balance of power and weaken US deterrence.
motion_areas: TH, as the United States, would de-escalate the war with Iran
THBT the US should prioritize great-power competition over Middle East intervention
THP a world where states can more easily wind down foreign wars despite alliance commitments

cards.title: Lebanon’s ‘Ceasefire’ Fails to Protect Civilians as Israel Keeps Hitting Children and Displacing Families
cards.background: Save the Children said Israeli attacks on Lebanon killed or injured more than four children per day on average during the first 25 days of the ceasefire that began on April 16. Citing Lebanon’s Health Ministry, the group said at least 22 children were killed and 89 injured in that period, bringing the total number of children killed since the renewed escalation on March 2 to almost 200, with about 2,900 people killed overall. More than one million people have been displaced, about 125,000 are living in collective shelters, and 44,800 of those shelter residents are children. Lebanon and Israel are due to hold direct talks in Washington, DC, on Thursday and Friday aimed at ending the war and discussing Hezbollah’s disarmament.

prop_args.thesis: A ceasefire that still produces daily child casualties is not a ceasefire in any meaningful sense, and the international community should treat Israel as violating the truce and prioritize civilian protection over vague de-escalation language.
mechanisms: First, the continued strikes destroy the credibility of any negotiated pause. This is because (1) civilians see no practical difference between 'war' and 'ceasefire' when children are still being killed and injured, (2) local compliance with future agreements collapses when one side is perceived to violate the deal with impunity, and (3) mediators lose leverage if they cannot enforce even the most basic civilian protections.

Second, the humanitarian harm compounds rapidly because displacement does not stop when the shooting slows. Three reasons: one, more than one million people have already been displaced, two, 125,000 people are in overcrowded shelters with poor sanitation, and three, 44,800 children in shelters face higher risks of disease, trauma, and interrupted schooling.

Third, this creates a political trap that prolongs the conflict. This matters because (1) every civilian death hardens Lebanese public opinion against compromise, (2) Hezbollah can use ongoing attacks to justify retaining its arsenal as 'protection,' and (3) the more the war is framed as existential, the harder it becomes for Washington talks to produce a durable settlement.

opp_args.thesis: Israel’s continued strikes are a necessary part of degrading Hezbollah’s military capacity, and a temporary truce that leaves Hezbollah armed and operational is strategically unstable.
mechanisms: First, the ceasefire may be conditional rather than absolute, so strikes can be justified as enforcement against violations. Numbered reasons: (1) Israel says it has hit more than 1,100 sites since mid-April, claiming Hezbollah is the target, (2) if Hezbollah continues to operate from civilian areas, Israel argues it cannot be expected to absorb attacks passively, and (3) allowing armed groups to reconstitute during a pause can make the next war larger and deadlier.

Second, pressure on Hezbollah may be the only path to a real settlement. Numbered reasons: (1) Hezbollah has explicitly said it will not surrender its weapons, (2) if negotiations do not change that fact, any ceasefire becomes a mere pause before renewed conflict, and (3) forcing disarmament onto the agenda may be necessary to protect both Israeli and Lebanese civilians in the long run.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether ongoing strikes are a proportionate enforcement tool or proof that the ceasefire is hollow. The prop side wins if the round is about civilian protection and the legitimacy of peace processes; the opp side has structural advantage only if it proves Hezbollah’s military presence makes any pause non-credible and that short-term harm is outweighed by preventing a larger future war.
motion_areas: TH, as an international mediator, would prioritize civilian protection over ceasefire enforcement against armed groups
THBT temporary ceasefires that do not stop civilian casualties should be treated as failed agreements
THP a world where peace talks require immediate and verifiable protection of civilians before disarmament negotiations

cards.title: UK Bank Tax Hikes Threaten to Push JPMorgan’s London HQ Investment Offshore
cards.background: Jamie Dimon said that if the UK raises taxes on banks after a change in government, JPMorgan could scrap plans to invest billions of dollars in a new London headquarters in Canary Wharf. The warning came in an interview with Francine Lacqua on Bloomberg Open Interest on 2026-05-12. The article frames the decision as a direct response to the UK tax environment and the political risk of future bank levies.

prop_args.thesis: Threatening higher bank taxes can deter large financial-sector investment and push capital formation, jobs, and headquarters functions out of London.
mechanisms: First, higher bank taxes raise the expected post-tax return on long-lived fixed investments, so firms delay or cancel projects. This is because (1) headquarters builds are sunk-cost commitments, (2) banks can compare London against rival hubs like New York, Dublin, Frankfurt, and Paris, and (3) even a small tax increase can flip a marginal location decision when the project is measured in billions.

Second, the threat of future tax hikes increases policy uncertainty, which is often more damaging than the tax rate itself. Three reasons: one, firms discount jurisdictions where rules can change after an election; two, uncertainty raises the hurdle rate for capital allocation; three, it encourages firms to keep high-value functions mobile rather than anchoring them in the UK.

Third, losing a flagship HQ has multiplier effects far beyond the building itself. This matters because (1) headquarters concentrate legal, compliance, trading, and executive roles, (2) those roles generate spillovers for local services, contractors, and professional firms, and (3) once a global bank shifts incremental investment elsewhere, London’s ecosystem becomes less attractive for other financial institutions too.

opp_args.thesis: The UK should not let one bank’s relocation threat dictate tax policy, because bank taxes can raise revenue and preserve the state’s bargaining power without causing a mass exodus.
mechanisms: First, banks are relatively immobile compared with the profits they generate, so governments can tax some of the rents without losing the entire industry. One, major banks still need access to London’s legal system, talent pool, time zone, and market infrastructure; two, a headquarters threat may be leverage in negotiations rather than a credible full exit; three, even if one project is delayed, the broader sector may remain because the UK offers unique clustering advantages.

Second, higher bank taxes can be justified on distributional and fiscal grounds, especially after crises or periods of elevated profits. Three reasons: one, banks benefit from implicit state backstops and systemic support; two, the public bears downside risk when finance destabilizes the economy; three, extra revenue can fund public services or reduce deficits, which may outweigh the loss of one investment project.

Third, the threat may be overstated because firms often use tax warnings strategically. This is because (1) CEOs have incentives to lobby against future regulation, (2) headline threats can be aimed at shaping political debate rather than reflecting a final capital-allocation decision, and (3) large multinationals usually diversify their footprint, so a cancelled HQ does not necessarily mean a full withdrawal from London.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether bank taxes meaningfully change mobile capital allocation or whether they mainly capture rents from a sector that is still locked into London’s ecosystem. Prop wins if the round is about marginal investment and long-run competitiveness; opp wins if the round is about fiscal sovereignty and the credibility of bank exit threats.
motion_areas: TH, as the UK government, would impose higher taxes on banks
THBT governments should prioritize retaining financial-sector investment over taxing banks more heavily
THP a world where major financial hubs can credibly threaten to relocate in response to tax policy

cards.title: US-Iran Ceasefire Collapses Into Coercive Stalemate as Both Sides Reject Concessions
cards.background: The article reports that the 10-week war between the US and Iran remains in an uneasy ceasefire, but negotiations are stalling. President Donald Trump rejected Iran’s latest offer, calling it a “piece of garbage,” and said the ceasefire was on “life support.” Bloomberg notes that both sides appear unwilling to make concessions, leaving the truce fragile and the conflict unresolved.

prop_args.thesis: Rejecting Tehran’s offer is strategically correct because it prevents the US from locking in a weak settlement that rewards escalation and preserves Iranian leverage.
mechanisms: First, refusing a bad deal preserves bargaining power. This is because (1) Iran’s offer likely reflects its current battlefield position, (2) accepting it would signal that violence produces diplomatic gains, and (3) future adversaries would infer that the US can be pressured into concessions under fire.

Second, a hard line deters repeat coercion. Three reasons: one, it raises the expected cost of using proxies, missiles, or escalation to extract concessions; two, it reassures allies that the US will not trade away security for short-term calm; three, it reduces the risk of a precedent where ceasefires become cover for rearmament.

Third, maintaining pressure can improve the eventual settlement. This matters because a ceasefire on unfavorable terms can freeze an unstable status quo, whereas sustained leverage may force Iran to accept verifiable limits, inspections, or security guarantees that are actually enforceable.

opp_args.thesis: Rejecting Iran’s offer is reckless because it prolongs a war that neither side can decisively win and increases the risk of regional spillover.
mechanisms: First, prolonging the stalemate increases human and material costs. One, every additional week of conflict creates more civilian casualties and infrastructure damage; two, it deepens economic disruption through shipping, energy, and insurance shocks; three, it makes de-escalation politically harder because leaders become trapped by sunk costs and domestic hawks.

Second, the refusal weakens the ceasefire architecture. One, if the truce is already on “life support,” public rejection signals that diplomacy is dead; two, that encourages hardliners on both sides to resume attacks as the default bargaining tool; three, it raises the probability of miscalculation, accidental escalation, or third-party involvement.

Third, the US may be overestimating its leverage. One, if Iran believes it can survive longer than Washington expects, pressure tactics fail; two, allies may not sustain support for an open-ended confrontation; three, a collapsed truce can produce a worse deal later, after more destruction and less trust.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether leverage or escalation risk dominates. Pro wins if the round is about preventing moral hazard and avoiding a capitulation deal; opp wins if the round is about the immediate human and strategic costs of keeping a fragile truce alive while neither side concedes.
motion_areas: TH, as the United States, would reject Iran’s latest ceasefire offer
THBT states should not negotiate with adversaries while active hostilities continue
THP a world where ceasefires are only accepted if they include enforceable concessions from both sides

cards.title: Israeli West Bank Violence Normalizes a Weekly Child Death Toll and Deepens Occupation Instability
cards.background: On 12 May 2026, Al Jazeera reported UN claims that Israeli military forces and settlers have killed at least one Palestinian child per week on average in the occupied West Bank since the start of 2025. UNICEF official James Elder publicly condemned the trend and urged Israeli authorities to uphold children’s rights. The article frames the issue as part of an escalating toll in the West Bank under occupation, involving both state forces and settlers.

prop_args.thesis: The weekly killing of Palestinian children in the West Bank is evidence that occupation has become a self-reinforcing system of dehumanization that will only worsen without external pressure.
mechanisms: First, the pattern normalizes lethal force against civilians, especially minors. This is because (1) repeated killings lower the political and moral cost of violence for soldiers and settlers, (2) the absence of meaningful punishment signals impunity, and (3) civilians adapt by expecting arbitrary force, which makes everyday life more dangerous and unstable.

Second, it radicalizes the next generation and destroys any remaining trust in legal or diplomatic processes. Three reasons: one, families who lose children are more likely to support resistance or revenge politics; two, children growing up under constant threat internalize the conflict as existential rather than negotiable; three, moderates lose credibility when they cannot protect basic safety.

Third, the humanitarian toll compounds into long-term political instability. This matters because children killed or traumatized today become a generation with worse education, worse mental health, and fewer economic prospects, which increases recruitment into militant networks and makes a future two-state or negotiated settlement harder to sustain.

opp_args.thesis: The reported deaths are tragic, but they do not by themselves prove a strategic shift or justify broad conclusions about the conflict’s trajectory.
mechanisms: First, casualty statistics can be politically contested and context-dependent. One, the UN and media reports may not distinguish clearly between combat situations, crossfire, and deliberate targeting; two, isolated figures do not establish intent or policy; three, the underlying conflict dynamics may be driven more by militant activity, raids, and security operations than by a new doctrine of child targeting.

Second, external condemnation may have limited leverage over Israeli behavior. One, Israel has strong domestic security incentives and can absorb diplomatic criticism; two, international actors are divided and often unwilling to impose costs; three, without credible enforcement, moral outrage may not change facts on the ground and can even harden positions by strengthening siege mentalities.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether this is treated as an isolated atrocity or as evidence of a broader occupation logic that is producing predictable civilian harm. Prop wins if it can show the pattern is systematic and self-perpetuating; opp wins if it can reframe the numbers as tragic but insufficient to prove policy change or strategic significance.
motion_areas: TH, as the UN, would impose stronger sanctions on Israel over West Bank civilian deaths
THBT external actors should condition military aid on civilian protection in occupied territories
THP a world where international institutions can credibly punish child killings in occupied territories
